questions.question: What is a "hook" in a presentation?
options: An attention-grabbing opening, like a question, statistic or short story
The last sentence of the conclusion
A type of visual aid
A pause in the middle of the talk
questions.explanation: A hook grabs the audience's attention at the start - for example a surprising statistic, a question or an anecdote.

questions.question: What does the rule "Tell them what you're going to tell them, tell them, then tell them what you told them" describe?
options: The structure of a presentation: preview, main points, summary
How to gossip politely
How to repeat yourself to fill time
How to answer questions from the audience
questions.explanation: This classic rule describes presentation structure: preview your points in the introduction, present them in the body, and summarise them in the conclusion.

questions.question: Why is eye contact important when presenting?
options: It connects you with the audience and makes you seem confident
It helps you read your script faster
It is only important for teachers
It makes the presentation shorter
questions.explanation: Eye contact builds a connection with the audience and signals confidence. Staring at your notes or the screen weakens your delivery.

questions.question: What does "less is more" mean for presentation slides?
options: Use few words and simple visuals instead of crowded slides full of text
Use as many slides as possible
Never use slides at all
Put your whole script on the slides
questions.explanation: Good slides support your talk with key words and images. Slides crammed with text make the audience read instead of listening to you.

questions.question: Which of these should you AVOID when delivering a presentation?
options: Reading your entire script word for word from the paper
Speaking clearly and loudly enough
Using natural gestures
Pausing to let points sink in
questions.explanation: Reading word for word kills eye contact and engagement. Use cue cards with key words and speak as freely as possible.
